item.title: Deepseek-moe
item.description:
The transition from the dense DeepSeek-LLM 67B to DeepSeekMoE marks the architectural pivot that defined all of DeepSeek’s later flagship models (DeepSeek-V2, V3, and R1).

While standard Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures—like Mixtral 8x7B or Switch Transformer—simply swap dense Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs) for a small bank of large sub-networks, DeepSeek discovered severe structural flaws in this setup. DeepSeekMoE re-architected the MoE layer around two core principles: fine-grained expert segmentation and shared expert isolation.

1. The Bottlenecks of Traditional MoE Architectures

Conventional MoEs divide the FFN layer into NNN experts (typically N=8N = 8N=8) and activate the top-KKK experts (typically K=2K = 2K=2) per token. DeepSeek identified two fundamental limitations in this paradigm:

  1. Knowledge Hybridity (Lack of Specialization): Because K=2K=2K=2 is so small, each routed expert is forced to learn a vast, overlapping mixture of broad concepts (e.g., syntax, grammar, basic facts) rather than truly specializing in narrow domains (e.g., Python recursion, organic chemistry, or legal reasoning).
  2. Combinatorial Constraint: With N=8N=8N=8 and K=2K=2K=2, the router can only produce: (82)=28 possible expert combinations \binom{8}{2} = 28 \text{ possible expert combinations} (28​)=28 possible expert combinations This severely caps the expressive capacity of the model for diverse tokens.
  3. Knowledge Redundancy: Multiple experts end up wasting capacity re-learning the exact same ubiquitous, cross-domain background knowledge.

2. The Core Mechanics of Fine-Grained Routing

DeepSeek addressed this by dividing the standard expert size into significantly smaller slices and activating proportionally more of them, keeping total activated FLOPs constant.

Traditional MoE (e.g., Mixtral 8x7B):
Input Token ──► [ Router: Top-2 of 8 ] ──► [ Large Expert 1 ] + [ Large Expert 4 ]
Combinations: 28
DeepSeekMoE Fine-Grained:
Input Token ──► [ Shared Experts (Always ON) ] ───────────────┐
└──► [ Router: Top-m of N (e.g., Top-8 of 64) ] ──┴──► Combined Output
Combinations: > 4.4 Billion

A. Fine-Grained Expert Segmentation

Instead of assigning an intermediate hidden dimension dffnd_{\text{ffn}}dffn​ to a single expert, DeepSeek divides it by a splitting factor mmm:

  • Each expert’s intermediate dimension becomes dffnm\frac{d_{\text{ffn}}}{m}mdffn​​.
  • To preserve the exact same compute budget per token, the number of activated routed experts scales from KKK to m×Km \times Km×K.
  • Total available experts increases from NNN to m×Nm \times Nm×N.

The Combinatorial Explosion:

If m=4m = 4m=4, an N=16,K=2N=16, K=2N=16,K=2 system becomes N=64,K=8N=64, K=8N=64,K=8:

(648)≈4.42×109 combinations \binom{64}{8} \approx 4.42 \times 10^9 \text{ combinations} (864​)≈4.42×109 combinations

By expanding the pool of available pathways from 28 to over 4.4 billion, the model can assemble specialized micro-circuits custom-tailored to nuanced token contexts, drastically reducing knowledge hybridity.

B. Shared Expert Isolation

To eliminate redundancy, DeepSeek isolates a fixed set of KsK_sKs​ shared experts that remain permanently active for every single token, bypassing the router entirely:

ht=ut+∑i=1KsFFNishared(ut)+∑j∈Top-Krgj,t⋅FFNjrouted(ut) \mathbf{h}_t = \mathbf{u}_t + \sum_{i=1}^{K_s} \text{FFN}_i^{\text{shared}}(\mathbf{u}_t) + \sum_{j \in \text{Top-}K_r} g_{j,t} \cdot \text{FFN}_j^{\text{routed}}(\mathbf{u}_t) ht​=ut​+i=1∑Ks​​FFNishared​(ut​)+j∈Top-Kr​∑​gj,t​⋅FFNjrouted​(ut​)

Where:

  • ut\mathbf{u}_tut​ is the input representation of token ttt.
  • FFNishared\text{FFN}_i^{\text{shared}}FFNishared​ processes universal common-sense patterns, punctuation, grammar, and generic sentence framing.
  • FFNjrouted\text{FFN}_j^{\text{routed}}FFNjrouted​ contains the fine-grained routed experts, which now only activate for domain-specific features.
  • gj,tg_{j,t}gj,t​ is the normalized routing weight computed over the selected top-KrK_rKr​ candidates.

3. Transitioning the Architecture: Dense 67B to MoE

To prove the paradigm, DeepSeek designed comparative models directly against the DeepSeek-LLM dense baselines:

Architecture Metric DeepSeek-LLM (Dense Baseline) DeepSeekMoE 16B Scaled DeepSeekMoE (V2 Base)
Total Parameters 7B (or 67B) 16.4B 236B
Activated Parameters / Token 7B (or 67B) 2.8B 21B
Routing Setup None (Dense FFN) 1 Shared + 64 Routed (Top-8 active) 2 Shared + 160 Routed (Top-6 active)
Compute Efficiency Baseline (1×1\times1×) ~40% compute of 7B dense ~30% compute of 67B dense
Performance Benchmark Baseline Matches/beats 7B dense Surpasses 67B dense

Why the Transition Succeeded:

  1. Parameter Decoupling: In the dense 67B model, scaling knowledge required scaling FLOPs linearly on every token. With fine-grained MoE, DeepSeek decoupled memory capacity (total parameters) from inference execution cost (active parameters).
  2. No Routing Collapse: Smaller, fine-grained experts combined with dedicated shared experts eliminated routing bottlenecks where one or two “celebrity experts” hog all the tokens, leading to far more uniform token distribution across hardware devices.

This fine-grained routing blueprint, validated in the January 2024 paper, served directly as the execution engine for DeepSeek-V2 and V3, allowing V3 to scale to 671B total parameters while activating only 37B per token.

item.title: Deepseek-v1
item.description:
DeepSeek-LLM: Scaling Open-Source Language Models with Longtermism (January 5, 2024) serves as DeepSeek’s foundational technical paper. It established both the empirical methodology and the engineering infrastructure that later underpinned models like DeepSeekMoE, DeepSeek-V2/V3, and DeepSeek-R1.

1. Motivation: Why “Longtermism”?

At the time of release, many open-source models scaled parameters by strictly copying LLaMA or following standard Chinchilla-scaling recipes without testing the limits of data-to-parameter saturation. DeepSeek approached scaling with two specific long-term goals:

  1. Rethink Scaling Laws Under Variable Data Quality: Systematically derive how hyperparameter selection (batch size, learning rate) and compute-optimal parameter-to-data allocation shift as data quality improves.
  2. Build Continuous Pre-Training Infrastructure: Move away from one-off, static model checkpoints by introducing training dynamics (such as multi-step learning rate schedules) that allow weights to be reused and expanded as more high-quality data arrives.

2. Empirical Scaling Laws & Key Findings

A. Hyperparameter Scaling Laws

Before scaling up to 7B and 67B parameter models, the authors evaluated hundreds of small-scale training runs across compute budgets from 101710^{17}1017 to 102010^{20}1020 FLOPs to establish exact power-law trends for learning rate (η\etaη) and batch size (BBB):

  • Optimal Batch Size (BBB): Monotonically grows as compute budget (CCC) increases.
  • Optimal Learning Rate (η\etaη): Monotonically decays as compute budget (CCC) increases.
  • Tolerance Basin: Generalization loss remained within 0.25% of the theoretical optimum across a relatively broad hyperparameter envelope, giving engineering flexibility when fitting models onto cluster hardware.

B. The Impact of Data Quality on Scaling Laws

A major discovery in this paper was that data quality fundamentally changes the optimal ratio between parameters (NNN) and data tokens (DDD):

  • When data quality is relatively low or noisy, optimal compute allocation favors scaling model size faster than token count, as larger models better absorb noisy signals.
  • As data quality improves via aggressive filtering, deduplication, and synthetic curation, the optimal frontier shifts: the model can extract information efficiently from significantly more tokens per parameter without premature loss saturation.
  • This justified training their 7B and 67B models on 2 trillion tokens—well beyond the canonical 20 tokens-per-parameter Chinchilla ratio.

3. Model Architecture & Pipeline Design

DeepSeek adopted a modern dense Transformer backbone with targeted structural modifications:

Specification DeepSeek 7B DeepSeek 67B
Layers 30 95
Hidden Dimension (dmodeld_{\text{model}}dmodel​) 4096 8192
Attention Heads (Q/KVQ/KVQ/KV) 32 / 32 (MHA) 64 / 8 (GQA)
Intermediate FFN Dim 11,008 27,648
Context Length 4,096 tokens 4,096 tokens
Vocabulary Size 102,400 tokens 102,400 tokens

Structural Highlights:

  • 95-Layer Depth for 67B: Rather than using the typical 80-layer layout seen in models like LLaMA-2 70B, DeepSeek opted for 95 layers. This odd layer depth was specifically selected to divide evenly across 3D-parallel pipeline stages while favoring depth-over-width inductive bias for symbolic and logical reasoning.
  • Grouped-Query Attention (GQA): 67B used 8 KV heads with 64 query heads (8:1 ratio) to cut KV cache memory consumption during decoding, whereas the 7B model retained standard Multi-Head Attention (MHA).
  • Pre-Norm + SwiGLU + RoPE: Followed standard pre-normalization with RMSNorm, SwiGLU non-linearities, and Rotary Position Embeddings.

4. Training Dynamics & The Multi-Step Learning Rate Schedule

Most pre-trained LLMs utilize a Cosine Learning Rate schedule with warmup, which decays the learning rate to near-zero at a pre-set step count. The paper points out two drawbacks of cosine decay:

  1. It commits the team to an exact token budget upfront.
  2. Extending training past the schedule’s end requires clumsy restarts or causes loss instability.

To support their “longtermism” philosophy, DeepSeek introduced a Multi-Step Learning Rate Scheduler for pre-training:

  • Warmup: Linear warmup over the first 2,000 steps to peak LR.
  • Constant High LR: Maintained steady peak learning rate through 80% of the training budget.
  • Step 1 Decay: At 80% of tokens, LR steps down to 31.6% (1/101/\sqrt{10}1/10​) of maximum.
  • Step 2 Decay: At 90% of tokens, LR steps down to 10% of maximum.

The authors proved that this multi-step schedule achieves a final validation loss virtually identical to a cosine schedule, while keeping the model in a high-learning state for the majority of the training run so additional token sets can be appended without destabilizing convergence.

5. Pre-Training Corpus & Alignment (SFT + DPO)

  • 2.0 Trillion Tokens: Pre-trained on a bilingual dataset (English and Chinese). The data pipeline was organized into three distinct phases: deduplication, filtering (linguistic heuristics and information-density scoring), and remixing (balancing code, scientific text, and informal forum discussions).
  • Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT): Fine-tuned across ~1.5 million instruction instances covering coding, conversational dialogue, reasoning, and multi-turn math.
  • Direct Preference Optimization (DPO): DeepSeek applied DPO directly to the SFT base using a batch size of 512 and a learning rate of 5×10−65 \times 10^{-6}5×10−6. They found that DPO notably boosted open-ended generation, nuance, and human evaluation scores while preserving performance on standard deterministic benchmarks.

6. Results and Benchmark Impact

  • Beating LLaMA-2 70B: Despite having slightly fewer parameters (67B vs. 70B) and being trained on 2T tokens, DeepSeek-LLM 67B outperformed LLaMA-2 70B across coding (HumanEval), mathematics (GSM8K, MATH), and standard reasoning benchmarks.
  • Chat Competitiveness: In Chinese and English open-ended evaluations, DeepSeek-LLM 67B Chat surpassed GPT-3.5, marking DeepSeek’s entrance as a top-tier open-weight model developer.

item.title: Deepseek-v2
item.description:
The paper “DeepSeek-V2: A Strong, Economical, and Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Language Model” (DeepSeek-AI, May 2024) introduced a 236B-parameter Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) transformer that drastically lowered training costs and inference serving overhead. With 236B total parameters and only 21B activated parameters per token, DeepSeek-V2 achieved performance competitive with contemporary closed and open front-runners while cutting KV cache memory requirements by 93.3% and boosting generation throughput by 5.76×.

Its core architectural breakthroughs are Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) and the DeepSeekMoE architecture.

1. Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA)

Standard Multi-Head Attention (MHA) and Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) run into heavy memory bandwidth bottlenecks during autoregressive generation because they must cache uncompressed Key and Value states across all layers. GQA reduces cache size by forcing heads to share keys and values, which can compromise representational capacity.

Syntaxradar

DeepSeek-V2 resolved this by projecting Keys and Values into low-rank compressed latent spaces.

arXiv

A. Low-Rank Key-Value Joint Compression

Instead of caching KKK and VVV vectors for all heads, the model projects the hidden representation ht∈Rdh_t \in \mathbb{R}^dht​∈Rd into a single compressed latent vector ctKV∈Rdc\mathbf{c}_{t}^{KV} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_c}ctKV​∈Rdc​ (where dc≪nhdhd_c \ll n_h d_hdc​≪nh​dh​):

ctKV=WDKVht \mathbf{c}_t^{KV} = W_{DKV} h_t ctKV​=WDKV​ht​

During generation, only ctKV\mathbf{c}_t^{KV}ctKV​ is retained in the KV cache. When computing attention, the model up-projects the cached latent into the attention keys and values on the fly:

arXiv

ktC=WUKctKV,vtC=WUVctKV \mathbf{k}_t^C = W_{UK} \mathbf{c}_t^{KV}, \quad \mathbf{v}_t^C = W_{UV} \mathbf{c}_t^{KV} ktC​=WUK​ctKV​,vtC​=WUV​ctKV​

Because matrix multiplication is associative, the up-projection matrix WUKW_{UK}WUK​ can be absorbed into the Query projection during inference, computing dot products directly against the low-rank latent vector to save FLOPs and memory access.

B. Decoupled Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE)

A major mathematical challenge with low-rank Key projection is that Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) are position-dependent and cannot be commutatively combined through a linear down-/up-projection matrix. DeepSeek solved this by decoupling content and position:

  • Key: Concatenates an up-projected content key with an explicit, low-dimensional RoPE key carrying positional information: kt,i=[kt,iC;RoPE(ktR)] \mathbf{k}_{t, i} = [\mathbf{k}_{t, i}^C ; \text{RoPE}(\mathbf{k}_t^R)] kt,i​=[kt,iC​;RoPE(ktR​)]
  • Query: Similarly projected into compressed latent space, up-projected to content queries, and concatenated with a RoPE query: qt,i=[qt,iC;RoPE(qt,iR)] \mathbf{q}_{t, i} = [\mathbf{q}_{t, i}^C ; \text{RoPE}(\mathbf{q}_{t, i}^R)] qt,i​=[qt,iC​;RoPE(qt,iR​)]

The total cached footprint per token per layer drops from 2nhdh2 n_h d_h2nh​dh​ down to just (dc+dhR)(d_c + d_h^R)(dc​+dhR​), reducing KV cache memory by 93.3% compared to standard MHA.

Syntaxradar

2. DeepSeekMoE Architecture

Conventional MoEs (such as Mixtral 8x7B) split the MLP into a few large experts (e.g., 8 experts, choosing top-2). DeepSeek argued that this granularity is too coarse, limiting the combinatorial combinations of knowledge and causing individual experts to overlap in responsibility.

DeepSeek-V2 implements two foundational MoE principles:

┌───────── Input Token x ─────────┐
│ │
▼ ▼
┌───────────────────────┐ ┌───────────────────────┐
│ Shared Experts │ │ Routed Experts │
│ (Always Activated) │ │ (Fine-Grained Top-m) │
│ [Expert 1, 2, ...] │ │ [Expert 1, 2, ..., N] │
└───────────┬───────────┘ └───────────┬───────────┘
│ │
└───────────────┬─────────────────┘
▼
Fused Output
  1. Fine-Grained Expert Segmentation: Instead of NNN standard-sized experts, DeepSeek divides expert capacity into mNmNmN smaller experts (each having 1/m1/m1/m the hidden dimension) and activates mkmkmk of them. DeepSeek-V2 scales this to 160 routed experts, selecting 6 routed experts per token. This vastly expands the combinatorial flexibility of expert coordination without increasing active compute.
  2. Dedicated Shared Experts: A subset of experts (2 shared experts) is permanently active for every token, bypassing the router.
    • Why this matters: In standard MoEs, generalist knowledge (syntax, standard grammar, formatting) ends up redundantly learned across many routed experts. Isolating shared parameters forces common representations into the shared experts, freeing routed experts to specialize strictly in distinct semantic domains.

The output for token xxx is:

y=∑i=1NsSharedExperti(x)+∑j∈Top-Kgj(x)⋅RoutedExpertj(x) \mathbf{y} = \sum_{i=1}^{N_s} \text{SharedExpert}_i(x) + \sum_{j \in \text{Top-}K} g_j(x) \cdot \text{RoutedExpert}_j(x) y=i=1∑Ns​​SharedExperti​(x)+j∈Top-K∑​gj​(x)⋅RoutedExpertj​(x)

3. Structural Specifications & Parameter Count

Specification Dimension / Value
Total Parameters 236B
Active Parameters / Token 21B
Number of Layers 60
Hidden Dimension (dmodeld_{\text{model}}dmodel​) 5120
Attention Heads (nhn_hnh​) 128
Head Dimension (dhd_hdh​) 128
KV Compression Dimension (dcd_cdc​) 512
Decoupled RoPE Dimension (dhRd_h^RdhR​) 64
Shared Experts 2
Routed Experts 160 (Top-6 routed per token)
Context Window 128K tokens (via YaRN extension)

4. Load Balancing & Training Dynamics

To prevent routing collapse across 160 fine-grained experts, DeepSeek-V2 avoided device-level hard capacity factors (which drop tokens and hurt quality) and instead used a multi-tier loss formulation:

  • Expert-Level Balance Loss (Lexp\mathcal{L}_{\text{exp}}Lexp​): Penalizes routing probability skew across individual experts.
  • Device-Level Balance Loss (Ldev\mathcal{L}_{\text{dev}}Ldev​): Groups experts across physical GPUs/nodes and penalizes imbalanced aggregate computation across accelerator devices, minimizing inter-device pipeline stalls.
  • Communication Optimization: By co-locating groups of routed experts and overlapping all-to-all communication with token computation kernels, the communication overhead typical of fine-grained MoE dispatch was mitigated on dual-ring cluster topologies.

5. Architectural Significance & Legacy

  • Inference Economy: Standard MoEs reduce training compute relative to parameter size, but during decoding they still suffer under full KV cache memory limits. MLA directly decoupled sequence memory from head width, enabling massive batch sizes and 128K context scaling on modest hardware clusters.
  • Foundation for V3 and R1: The twin innovations of MLA and fine-grained shared/routed MoE established the blueprint carried forward into DeepSeek-Coder-V2, DeepSeek-V3, and the DeepSeek-R1 reasoning series.

item.title: mHC
item.description:
Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) is an architectural framework introduced by DeepSeek-AI (mHC: Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections, arXiv:2512.24880) designed to scale and stabilize the macro-architecture of deep networks—particularly large language models.

It addresses fundamental training instabilities in multi-stream residual networks by enforcing geometric constraints on how residual information is routed across layers.

1. Background: From ResNets to Hyper-Connections (HC)

In standard Transformers and ResNets, a layer update follows a single residual stream:

xl+1=xl+F(xl,Wl) \mathbf{x}_{l+1} = \mathbf{x}_l + \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x}_l, \mathcal{W}_l) xl+1​=xl​+F(xl​,Wl​)

This identity shortcut (xl\mathbf{x}_lxl​) guarantees that:

  • Forward signals can pass unaltered without vanishing or exploding.
  • Gradients can flow backward across deep layers without attenuation (∂xl+1∂xl≈I\frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_{l+1}}{\partial \mathbf{x}_l} \approx \mathbf{I}∂xl​∂xl+1​​≈I).

The Hyper-Connections (HC) Generalization

To increase capacity without altering internal block FLOPs, recent work introduced Hyper-Connections (HC). Instead of a single residual vector, HC expands the residual pathway into nnn parallel streams:

xl+1=Hlresxl+(Hlpost)⊤F(Hlprexl,Wl) \mathbf{x}_{l+1} = \mathbf{H}_l^{\text{res}} \mathbf{x}_l + (\mathbf{H}_l^{\text{post}})^\top \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{H}_l^{\text{pre}} \mathbf{x}_l, \mathcal{W}_l) xl+1​=Hlres​xl​+(Hlpost​)⊤F(Hlpre​xl​,Wl​)

Where:

  • Hlpre∈R1×n\mathbf{H}_l^{\text{pre}} \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times n}Hlpre​∈R1×n: Reads and linearly mixes features from the nnn streams to feed into the computational block F\mathcal{F}F (e.g., Attention or FFN).
  • Hlpost∈R1×n\mathbf{H}_l^{\text{post}} \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times n}Hlpost​∈R1×n: Writes the output of the block back across the nnn streams.
  • Hlres∈Rn×n\mathbf{H}_l^{\text{res}} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}Hlres​∈Rn×n: Inter-stream residual routing matrix that mixes parallel streams directly.

2. The Problem with Unconstrained Hyper-Connections

While HC demonstrated empirical benefits on shallow setups, it breaks the identity mapping assumption in deep architectures:

  • In standard HC, the inter-stream matrix Hlres\mathbf{H}_l^{\text{res}}Hlres​ is an unconstrained linear transformation.
  • As signals propagate through LLL layers, the effective residual path is governed by the cumulative matrix product: ∏l=1LHlres \prod_{l=1}^L \mathbf{H}_l^{\text{res}} l=1∏L​Hlres​
  • Without constraints, eigenvalues deviating slightly from 1.01.01.0 compound exponentially. This causes:
    • Forward signal explosion or collapse: Feature norms either blow up or fade to zero.
      • Gradient instability: Backward gradients along the residual paths explode or vanish, preventing convergence in very deep or large-scale models.

3. DeepSeek’s Solution: Manifold Constraints (mHC)

DeepSeek’s core insight is that network stability is a geometric property. Instead of allowing arbitrary linear mixing, mHC constrains the connection matrices onto specific mathematical manifolds:

 ```

┌───────────────────────────────┐ │ Input Streams (x_l) │ └──────┬─────────────────┬──────┘ │ │ ▼ ▼ H_res (Doubly Stochastic) H_pre (Convex Weights) via Sinkhorn-Knopp │ │ ▼ │ ┌──────────────┐ │ │ Sub-Layer F │ │ └──────┬───────┘ │ │ │ ▼ │ H_post │ │ ▼ ▼ ┌───────────────────────────────┐ │ Output Streams (x_{l+1}) │ └───────────────────────────────┘


#### A. Doubly Stochastic Residual Mapping ($\mathbf{H}_l^{\text{res}}$)
mHC constrains $\mathbf{H}_l^{\text{res}}$ to the **Birkhoff polytope** (the set of doubly stochastic matrices):
1. **Non-negativity**: $\mathbf{H}_{ij} \ge 0$ (prevents destructive interference or sign inversion).
2. **Row Sums $= 1$**: $\sum_j \mathbf{H}_{ij} = 1$ ensures that the forward operation $\mathbf{H}_l^{\text{res}} \mathbf{x}_l$ is a strict convex combination of residual streams, conserving forward signal scale.
3. **Column Sums $= 1$**: $\sum_i \mathbf{H}_{ij} = 1$ ensures that during backpropagation, the incoming adjoint gradients are also convexly distributed, preventing gradient explosion.
**Key Mathematical Invariant (Closure):** Because the product of any two doubly stochastic matrices is itself doubly stochastic, the compound residual path across arbitrary layers:
$$
\mathbf{M}_{1 \to L} = \prod_{l=1}^L \mathbf{H}_l^{\text{res}}
$$
remains strictly doubly stochastic. This guarantees that identity-like conservation holds across arbitrary depth without norm distortion.
#### B. Projection via Sinkhorn–Knopp
To map unconstrained learned logits $\mathbf{S}_l \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ onto the Birkhoff polytope in a differentiable manner, DeepSeek applies the **Sinkhorn–Knopp algorithm**:
1. Compute elementwise exponentiation $\mathbf{P}^{(0)} = \exp(\mathbf{S}_l)$.
2. Alternately normalize rows and columns for a small number of iterations (e.g., 3–5 steps):
$$
\mathbf{P}^{(k+1/2)} = \mathbf{D}_{\text{row}}^{-1} \mathbf{P}^{(k)}, \quad \mathbf{P}^{(k+1)} = \mathbf{P}^{(k+1/2)} \mathbf{D}_{\text{col}}^{-1}
$$
*(Note: The paper also explores orthostochastic matrices derived via iterative Newton–Schulz steps as an alternative unitary-preserving geometry).*
#### C. Non-Negative Pre- and Post-Projections
$\mathbf{H}_l^{\text{pre}}$ and $\mathbf{H}_l^{\text{post}}$ are mapped via functions like softmax or non-negative normalizations to ensure that reading from and writing to the residual streams acts as smooth interpolation rather than divergent linear projection.
### 4\. Systems Optimization & Empirical Findings
Expanding residual channels multiplies the volume of activations transferred between layers, which could otherwise introduce substantial memory bandwidth and runtime bottlenecks. DeepSeek addresses this through co-designed systems engineering:
- **Kernel Fusion & Custom DSLs:** Using TileLang, mHC fuses the Sinkhorn–Knopp iterations, tensor contractions, and layer-norm operations into unified GPU kernels.
- **Overhead at Scale:** For an expansion factor of $n = 4$ streams, mHC adds only ~6.7% wall-clock training overhead while providing strictly stable convergence.
- **Scaling Behavior:** Models trained with mHC exhibit improved loss convergence rates compared to standard single-stream baselines at equal compute budgets, demonstrating that multi-stream residual routing can be scaled without architectural degradation.
